analysis.one_liner: Bans corporate executives and directors from trading their company's stock between a major event and its public disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the 118th Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies must file a Form 8-K report when major events happen—like an executive leaving, a bankruptcy, or a deal falling through. There is often a gap of days between the event and the public filing. This bill would require the SEC to write rules banning a company's officers and directors from buying or selling company stock during that gap, so insiders cannot profit on bad news (or good news) before the public knows. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday investors who buy and sell stocks without inside access. When executives can trade in the days between a corporate event and the public filing, they trade on information ordinary investors don't have yet, which shifts losses to outside shareholders. Closing that gap levels the field slightly for retirement savers and retail investors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday stock investors and retirement savers

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the SEC to require companies to maintain policies that prohibit executive officers and directors from trading the company's securities between the occurrence of a major reportable event and the filing of the Form 8-K disclosing it [S2].

It also closes a loophole in so-called 10b5-1 trading plans: executives could not adopt a pre-scheduled trading plan during the event-to-filing window to launder trades made on inside information [S2].
Events already announced publicly through a press release are exempted, so the rule targets only the window when the information is genuinely not yet public [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporate executives and directors of publicly traded companies, who would lose the ability to buy or sell their company's stock in the days between a material event and its public filing, forfeiting trades that can be profitable when markets react to the news.

drawbacks.text: The financial benefit to ordinary investors is modest: the event-to-filing gap is usually short, and broader insider-trading law already prohibits trading on material nonpublic information; this bill mainly closes one specific timing loophole [S2].
Compliance costs fall on public companies, which must build and maintain policies and controls to police executive trading during the blackout windows [S2].
Certain events a company chooses to announce via press release are exempted, which could give companies a route to narrow the rule's reach by announcing more events themselves [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real but narrow fairness problem: executives trading stock in the days between a corporate event and the public disclosure of it. The benefit to ordinary investors is real but modest, since insider trading is already broadly illegal—the bill just removes one timing loophole and the safe-harbor workaround. The cost is mainly compliance paperwork for companies. On balance it is a reasonable, low-cost fairness rule, not a major overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on September 19, 2024 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S4].
No further action was taken: the bill received no committee hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate executives and directors keep the ability to trade their company's stock during the window between a major event and its public disclosure. Everyday investors continue to bear the losses from those trades.

for.name: Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would require the SEC to ban executives and directors from trading during the event-to-disclosure window.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral; controls whether the bill gets a hearing or vote
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and never acted on it; no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the only sponsor was a Democrat, so the bill's partisan shape was never tested.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and directors of public companies
industries.note: The bill's rules would prohibit them from trading company stock in the window between a reportable event and the public 8-K filing, closing a window they can currently use to trade ahead of the market. Its defeat preserves that timing advantage over outside investors.

Companies would bear the cost of building trading policies and controls, but they are also the entities whose outside shareholders benefit from the rule. The bill also exempts investment companies and their advisers from the requirement.
The bill expressly exempts registered investment companies and their advisers, so their executives would face no new trading restrictions under these rules.
